utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Lucy Turner, who is a graduate of the University of East Anglia in philosophy and law and has been with my team since the beginning of the year. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue today, the Chamber was informed of the -- or rather inquired of the possibility of extended sitting today, but due to the Chamber's circumstances, it's not possible to have an extended sitting today. So I'll leave it to the parties how to proceed under the circumstances. Yes. Good morning, Mr. Orlovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There is a technical problem in the French booth. Their microphones are not working at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There is a technical problem in the French booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We think, Your Honour, that it is working now. 1, 2, 1, 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Judge Lattanzi is receiving the translation. Yes, Mr. Zec. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Orlovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We are hearing French on the English channel. Could you sort it out. If you could continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Orlovic.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You told us in your statement that you were a journalist at Sanski Most Radio in 1992. It is correct, is it, that after the take-over of the power in Sanski Most in late April 1992 and upon the orders of the Crisis Staff, you and Miodrag Despot took over the functioning of the Sanski Most Radio?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I start answering? I was employed with Radio Sanski Most, and I only continued to work there, not on anybody's orders. I just came to work like every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In question 22 of your statement, you were asked whether it is true that you received a telephone call to complain about the content of the radio programme as being Serb nationalist. You said this was not true and that the radio tried to be objective and up to date. The reality is, Mr. Orlovic, that after the take-over the radio was a Serb radio station controlled by the Crisis Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In response to question 76, you said that in June or July 1992 there was a tournament of peace held in Sanski Most where Muslims and Croats played basketball for peace. In fact, Mr. Orlovic, initiatives like this took place in the period before the take-over of the power in Sanski Most in April 1992, and you called the initiatives like this "peacenik hogwash"; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the board of directors of the women's basketball club Sana and together we organised the peace tournament. I can't remember anymore whether it was in June or July 1992. It was a long time ago. The tournament was very well attended and several Croat and Bosniak players also took part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In question 6 you were asked: "Did the Serbs in Sanski Most publicly state that 5.500 Serbs who were killed in the Second World War should be avenged or was there fear that history would repeat itself?" You said: "Absolutely not." And then you explained that there was fear among Serbs of a repetition of 1941. In fact, Mr. Orlovic, you were among those who were actively engaged in spreading the fear among the Serbs, saying that genocide against Serbs must not be repeated; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 11, the witness also said, and it's missing from the record, "it's not hogwash."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Orlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it's not hogwash or window dressing, because it's a very ugly term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now can you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Sanski Most in 1941 on the 1st and 2nd of August, 5.500 Serbs and Jews were killed. Many survived these atrocities. Some are descendents of the people who were killed. And all the time since that event to date, they counsel their descendents not to be fooled like they had been fooled, lest they be taken to execution sites and killed. So that fear really existed and it was a justified fear. There is nothing bad in the fear itself. Fear is necessary for survival. I personally never spread fear, and in fact, I wrote a book, accounts of people who survived Susnjar. And as somebody who is involved in that line of work in proving the truth, you cannot say that they are spreading fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have a look at 65 ter 25963. And this is an article from "Podgrmecke Novine."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We see your name on the top of the page. You wrote this article, Mr. Orlovic; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote that. But I can tell you straight away that all that is written here are not my words, because the person who edited this newspaper changed a lot and added words of his own. Later, if necessary, I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Well, let's see what it says. The article starts by saying: "Sanski Most has well learned its lesson from the Second World War. Five and a half thousand Serbs, and perhaps even more, were heinously killed at the hand of their neighbours - Muslims and Croats." A few lines below: "When the Ustasha serpent reared its head again and when the Serb people rose up in Krajina to save their lives, face and honour, the clouds of dark premonition crept in, slowly gathering over our parts too. The genocide must not be repeated - were the words being uttered by every Serb." This relates, Mr. Orlovic, to the Second World War and what, according to you, was about to happen to Serbs after Croatia and Bosnia moved for independence; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Genocide of the kind that happened in Susnjar must not repeat itself to no one, including the Serbs. There are many words here, passages added by the person who edited this newspaper, but the gist is true. At least my words, that it cannot be, it must not be repeated. It must not happen to anyone in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The second section you named "peacenik hogwash." You refer here to the winter of 1991 when, as you explain here, various meetings and rallies were held during this period. At the end of this section --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Which is English page 2, B/C/S second column.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: -- you say: "Apart from that struggle at the meetings, they developed a campaign of so-called 'peacenik' ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In English, second page:

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: "... they developed a campaign of so-called 'peacenik' whose objective was to deaden the Serb people after they acquire strong chains and halters. Afterwards it would be easier for them. Various meetings are held, which looked like hogwash. Proclamations are sent out, rallies organised, panels, petitions signed. One or two Serbs would stray among the 'peacenik' but would quickly get ahold of themselves and come back. The 'peaceniks' were the darkest and uglier side of the SDA and HDZ, which events would also confirm." This is, Mr. Orlovic, what you wrote regarding the peace rallies that took place before the take-over of the power in 1992 which you falsely represent in your statement as taking place after the take-over June or July 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a series of meetings, a series of rallies, and people showed up who later joined national ranks. So if you look at it that way, people were hypocritical. On the one hand, they were saying they want peace, and on the other hand they were working against peace. That's what it looked like at that time. And from where I'm sitting even now, when you look at it objectively, nothing really changed. Simply, hypocrisy ruled in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Here in this portion just above this same text, you describe Redzo Kurbegovic, from the SDA, as not the brightest spark. Hasib Komber [phoen], Refiris [phoen], Faik Biscevic, the fat and pumpkin-like, Ismet Sabic, a pockmarked, and you say other pitiful names. You say you were puzzled that the SDS was even talking to such people. This was your description, Mr. Orlovic, of members of other ethnic groups; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not really my description. I repeat, there was general propaganda prevailing at the time, and if you submit a story, a piece of writing somewhere, that text is subjected to all sorts of modifications. I did not put these epithets here. They must have been added. But I want to tell you something really important: Believing that one day the truth will finally prevail, I kept all these documents both in my work-place in the radio and at home. Unfortunately, on the 10th of October, 1995, the building of the radio was set on fire. And later --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Orlovic --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- also when the Muslim forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just about to say that if that hadn't happened, I would now have a very precious document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Orlovic. Please answer the question. Yes. Please continue, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Next section of this article you called: Sanski Most is Serb nevertheless. You start by saying: "The Serbian Democratic Party is working feverishly to pull the Serb people out from under the fierce Islamic clutches and Vatican knife." You talk here, Mr. Orlovic, about the events that took place in the period before April 1992 and leading up to the Serb take-over of Sanski Most; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These events happened in April and May and throughout 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Well, it's not throughout. This is up to April. And next section, which is English page 3, which is the last section of this article, you say: Life afterwards. And here you refer to 20 April 1992, and you say: "It is from the newly formed Crisis Staff that they are requesting that the problem should start. Miodrag Despot and I are at work. The programme starts with a delay and the radio airs for the first time as a Serb one. That day, as per arrangement, all the Muslims do not come into work in any of the companies ..." This is, Mr. Orlovic, about you taking over the functioning of the Sanski Most radio, 20 April 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says here is that I came to work on that day in April, like any other day, Miodrag Despot and I as journalists. And Muslims and Croats who had worked earlier in Radio Sanski Most had agreed out of fear or whatever reasons they had and didn't come to work, didn't show up. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this article, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6645, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: After the conflict started, you were part of the Sanski Most delegation visiting soldiers at the front lines together with other members of the municipal leadership, Rasula, Vrkes, Anicic [phoen], and others; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember I ever went with Rasula and Vrkes and Janicic [phoen] somewhere. But I did sometimes go to tour Serb lines, and my assignment was to see how people live in order that their families, their children and wives, may live peacefully and normally at home. But that I went with Rasula and the others, no, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 25982.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is a conclusion of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff from June 1992. And if you look at the document, it provides a list of people to go visit soldiers and your name is there; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's my name, but I didn't go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6646, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And while talking to soldiers, you discussed issues such as defending the Serb state and preventing genocide against Serbs; right? Mr. Orlovic --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: -- when you were went to see soldiers, you talked to them about issues such as defending Serb state, preventing genocide against Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't go together with these gentlemen into the field. I said I sometimes went as a journalist, as a reporter, only to meet with those people, to see how they lived and what they were doing so that their families could be in peace. But I didn't go with these gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I was not part of any forum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Orlovic, there are people who translate everything you say. When you finish your answer, you have to stop and wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Also hear him out, please. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is an article from "Podgrmecke Novine," interview with Miroslav Radakovic, chief of staff of the 6th Brigade. You wrote this article; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see my signature. Where does it say I wrote this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have next page in B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You see now at the end of the article your name.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then probably I did. If I read it, I would remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we go back the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And in the first paragraph of the article, it says: "Its fighters have defended the Serb people in the Krajina from resurrectment, Ustasha ghosts, and they have saved their hometown of Sanski Most from a new genocide, from a repetition of Susnjari, and then went on a glorious quest to liberate the Serbian lands." This is your comment, Mr. Orlovic, related to the topic you discussed with a soldier; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat again, there were various editors, and now I can't remember whether my text read exactly like this in the original. All that I published during the war can be called into question because there were always modifications made to my writing that I could not influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: At English page 2, in the B/C/S second column, under the section called "From Plitvice to Grabez," it says: "The political situation in these territories of ours had worsened around this period. Realising what was in store for the Serbian people, the brigade command was working harshly to set up a defence, for which they received huge support from the people, the SDS, and the authorities." This refers, Mr. Orlovic, to the period prior to the take-over of the power in the Sanski Most when the Serb people were being organised; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That relates to April, yes. No, the basis of all this, at that time, it was thought that strong organisation is necessary because people feared for their lives. They feared that 1941 would repeat itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Please keep in mind that we have your statement in evidence. You've explained a lot of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: At English page 4 and at the B/C/S last column, under the section called "Genocide Prevented," it says: "Against their will, our brigade's fighters were sucked into a bloody, ethnic, religious, and civil war." A few lines below, it says: "When the war started to rage in Croatia, dark clouds were also gathering over the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, where the Croat and Muslim factions tried to take advantage of the situation and subdue the Serb people. However, due to their historical experiences from 1914 and 1941, the people of the Krajina realised what kind of situation they were in, and organised themselves to defend the Serbian people and liquidate the extreme enemy groups that were openly trying to take over Serbian territories, subjecting them to unprecedented examples of genocide. It was simultaneously a warning to stop the dark forces of the past and prevent a repetition of terror and genocide."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Orlovic, this refers to the First and Second World War and the activities undertaken to organise Serbs to defend their territories from other ethnic groups, Muslims and Croats, as Bosnia moved for independence in 1990s; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what my collocutor said and that's what he thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this article, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6647, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Response to question 27 [Realtime transcript read in error "77"], you say that in a situation in which all PTT and road connections were cut, decisions were made in the SDS Municipal Board for the benefit of all. Mr. Orlovic, this Chamber has received evidence that Crisis Staff members were in communication with both the ARK and the SDS republican authorities during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is in P2613, P3399, and P3919.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So the reality is, Mr. Orlovic, after the take-over of the power in Sanski Most, the Crisis Staff continued to communicate with the regional and republican Serb authorities; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me whether the Crisis Staff continued to communicate? I don't know that. I was not a member of the Crisis Staff. I know that in spring, all communications - including telephone lines - were down or very bad. So if they did, I don't know how they managed. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you, yourself, were able to send news reports from Sanski Most to the mass media; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could sometimes. It depended on the communications. There were very few mass media who were willing to receive information from Sanski Most or any other places that were under Serb control. I was a correspondent for Radio Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's -- I'll show you one article.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I can't find the place where it says in paragraph 77 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- what has just been alleged. It says "77" in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And second of all, I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to allow the witness to answer. He has been interrupted too many times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, that's -- the Chamber is taking care of that matter. It was 27 that was referred to. By the way, do you have your statement with you, Mr. Orlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What number? What page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I was just checking. When necessary, it's okay for you to consult your statement when referred to by Mr. Zec. Yes, shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 05015. And this is an article from "Glas," dated 21 April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This article talks about the take-over of Sanski Most and the arrival of the 6th Brigade to the town. You wrote this article, Mr. Orlovic, that was published in "Glas"; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. They couldn't make it up, but I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Well, we see your name under the article.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this article, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where do we see his name?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Probably in English it's not translated, but if you look at the end of the first section in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we need a revised English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I think so, yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Also, Mr. President, I don't think that the article -- just simply because he wrote an article is enough to make something admissible unless we hear some question directed at the content of the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's about the communication, I take it? "Glas" is published where, Mr. Orlovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Orlovic, this was published in Banja Luka, "Glas"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was published in Banja Luka. Perhaps you would like to tell me how we reached Banja Luka, whether it was by phone or whether we travelled there. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6648, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Orlovic, you were --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, one more objection. I'm not sure that on page 12, line 22, that the document numbers have been properly recorded. The numbers do not meet our expectations, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably Mr. Zec could assist you out of the courtroom. That said, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Orlovic, you were appointed by the Crisis Staff to report on the situation in Sanski Most to the Serb mass media in Serbia and Serb claimed areas in Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I was appointed. However, I made sure to publicise everything that was going on in Sanski Most. People craved information. Whenever I could publish something, I did my best to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have a look at 65 ter 25973.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And these are conclusions of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff from May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We need to look at item number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And item number 9 says that information service reporting from Sanski Most for the RTV Banja Luka and the RTV Belgrade should be done by Predrag Predojevic and Mihajlo Orlovic. So your role, Mr. Orlovic, was to make sure that the interests and views of the Serb Crisis Staff were publicly presented; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff probably did deal with that, with those problems. However, it was my own initiative. I made arrangements with the materiel board of RT Banja Luka. I asked to be their correspondent. During the war I did only that. I was not engaged anywhere else. It was a good opportunity for me to show what was going on in Sanski Most. Myself and Predrag Predojevic were together at first and then he left the job and we were joined by a new colleague who recorded the shows instead of Predojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6649, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 25993. And now we're going to look at some of the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you're going to see on the screen a news report for a news programme called Dnevnik that was broadcast on 26 May 1992. So, Mr. Orlovic, you prepared a report that was broadcast on the radio, of which summary we see on the screen; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I think we lost the document. We need 65 ter -- yes. We need 65 ter 25993. It was there a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Orlovic, this is a --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is just a title.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct. That's what presenter on the radio would read into the news programme and they would play your report which is audio recorded, and we see here it's about one minute long. But this is the summary of your report from Sanski Most that you sent; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, this is a summary. I don't see anything bad here. Actually, it's all good because it's about disarming.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So it is not then true that communications were not possible. Not only they were possible but you personally were responsible for publicising the views and actions of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Communications were impaired. We had electricity by spoonfuls. When there was electricity, we could communicate, but those moments were rare. We had local links with Banja Luka. Only when the corridor of life was established and when we could communicate with Belgrade could we also communicate with Serbia and abroad. Our frequent communications with Banja Luka was reduced to actually taking our materials there by bus.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You cannot interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I don't follow. You should not interrupt the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness answered the question. There is no need for him to go on about [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I don't know where -- read his answer. Which one is unnecessary? "Our frequent communications with Banja Luka was reduced to actually taking our materials there by bus." So you find it unnecessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If in the interest of time, I think his first part of the answer was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we are losing more time. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I will tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6650, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We just saw your report of 26 May 1992, which was around the time the area of Sanski Most called Mahala was attacked by the Serb forces. You referred to Mahala in response to several questions put to you, question 12, 32, 55, 56. You say that you don't think there was any heavy shelling in Mahala. Mr. Orlovic, this Chamber has received evidence that Serb soldiers forced Mahala residents to gather at the training ground, following which Mahala was shelled and buildings burned down. Thousands of unarmed non-Serbs were detained and many killed in the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So it is not correct, Mr. Orlovic, that there was no heavy shelling of Mahala. Mahala was shelled, buildings were destroyed, and civilians killed. That was what happened there; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps two or three years later I passed through Mahala and I saw houses, which means that Mahala had not been burned. A few of the houses had been destroyed, perhaps later or maybe even during the operation when illegal arms were seized. I don't know what the operation was known as at the time. When things were happening in Mahala, journalists were not allowed access which means that we were not able to visit that part of the theater of war, and I don't mean the "theater of war" but this part or this area where this operation was ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's hear the Sanski Most radio broadcast from late May 1992 around the time Mahala was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is in P725 and we have provided the transcripts to the interpreters. The portion we will hear is at English page 7, B/C/S page 11 to 12 of the transcript. This clip is at 15 minutes and 13 seconds to 16 minutes and 21 seconds of the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... all the struggle and retaliation will be in vain. You are not capable of standing up to the forces of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the statement of the Serb armed forces command states. It adds, your resistance will force us to destroy and devastate your villages which means that you will not be able to live with us in these territories. If you do want to go on living in these territories, accept co-operation, hand over all the weapons and military equipment, and surrender to the Serb authorities all the extremists who forced you to fight. As long as one of you has a weapon, you risk the destruction of your houses and families, to collect all weapons and hand them over to the public security station or the Crisis Staff. The roads are gree, fire won't be opened until the deadline. The following villages have to hand over their weapons: Trnovo, Sasina, Sehovci, Poljak, Pobrijezje, Kijevo, Vrhpolje, Hrustovo, Skrljevita and Kruhari. Again, we call on you to be sensible and act as we did with Mahala. Arrest or bring the extremists who are forcing you to get killed to the public security station."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Orlovic, this was the reality. We heard on this radio broadcast that as long as one of you has a weapon, you risk the destruction of your houses and families. And the destruction of Mahala was used as an example and a threat to non-Serbs as to what awaited them; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was a threat or a warning. It's a matter of subjective assessment. I suppose it was a warning, according to which if something went wrong, things would go the way they would go. This was probably an announcement which was sent and aired on Radio Sanski Most and probably it was a warning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't say "destruction of Mahala," it says "you will force us to do what we did in Mahala." In the original, it doesn't say that Mahala was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It says "as we did with Mahala" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- that's all. Yes, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And the transcript also of the tape says, "You will force us to destroy and devastate your villages," among others things. May I continue, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: After Mahala, Mr. Orlovic, the Serb forces attacked other non-Serb forces such as Begejci and Hrustovo. After Serb forces entered Begejci, they rounded up non-Serb civilians and forced them to leave. Between 20 and 30 men were taken towards the Vrhpolje bridge, including Enes Dizdarevic [phoen], who was 16, and Cacir Begic [phoen], who was 75 at the time, and they shot them as they were ordered to jump into the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is in P691, P692, P48353.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: At Hrustovo, the Serb forces killed over 20 civilians that took shelter in the garage of Ibrahim Medanovic, including young children?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you knew, Mr. Orlovic, that ordinary civilians were killed in Sanski Most, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time there was a lot of rumor, a lot of propaganda. All the stories including murders, killings, and destruction, I always took them with a grain of salt. I never believed them. Even 20 years after the end of the war, I still don't believe that things like that happened. All the cases that did occur, they cannot be seen as falling under a system or part of some organised activity. Those were individual incidents that should be condemned. When you mentioned Hrustovo, let me give you just a few examples. In Hrustovo, in 1941, a lot of Serbs were killed. Zilhad Kljucanin wrote a book, "It is a Crime To Forget a Crime." There is another author whose name escapes me at the moment. It says in that book that on the 15th of April there was a parade of some 300 armed people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Orlovic, I think you are talking about 1941.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was in 1992. I have just moved on to 1992. I did mention 1941, but just in passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's keep on this topic. You say in response to question 12 that after Mahala, Muslim extremists who did not want to surrender weapons withdrew to Caplje and Hrustovo where the fighting with them continued. Mr. Orlovic, while you claim this happened, you reported to the Serb mass media on 29 May 1992 that it is -- that is between the attacks on Mahala and Hrustovo - that the situation in Sanski Most was calm but tense; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, calm but tense. Because nobody ever knew what was going on. We didn't know one day what would happen the next day. The situation was difficult and there was a lot of unrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 25994.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is another news reports of yours for 29 May 1992 saying that the situation in Sanski Most is mostly calm but there is a lot of tension. While we know, Mr. Orlovic, that Serb forces had already begun to destroy non-Serb villages to the ground, killing and detaining many; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent this report, I don't know to whom. Its objective was to calm the situation down, to eliminate fear. I wanted people to believe that life was still possible. And as to whether there was destruction, as you said it, and those are very serious words, and razing villages to the ground, none of the villages were leveled. It was two or three years later when abandoned house just fell into disrepair. Serb houses looked much worse, especially after the 10 October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6651, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's see what you wrote later in the mass media regarding these events?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 25965.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is another article of yours in "Podgrmecke Novine."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript perhaps. Line 10, it was not recorded that the witness mentioned a date when Serb houses looked much worse, and the date was 10 October 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be checked. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: English page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the section called "The fire spills over towards Vrhpolje," you say: "If any of the unfortunate Muslims who had realised that there would be no victory over the Serbs and who wanted peace tried to return weapons, they would be killed, even slaughtered by the extremists, something that Vrhpolje Hodja especially stood out in, that handful of the arrogant wretches with the Koran in their pockets and rifles in their hands, attacked the Serb soldiers who come to peacefully take over the weapons." So this is your story, Mr. Orlovic, regarding the victims of the Serb attack on Vrhpolje. You say the hodza killed them; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say that it was a Serb attack on the village. That's number one. Second of all, I repeat: There was a lot of rumor and propaganda. Many pieces of news that reached me came from people. I conveyed that news, but I was never in a situation to be able to check the veracity of such news.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the relevant Serbian part because that part is not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It's under the section: "Fire spills over towards Vrhpolje," and I read to the witness -- I read to him the relevant passage, so I don't see much need to wait more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it's always important to show the passage when you read out from the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And I believe I said -- but it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And I tender this article, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6652, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You said in response to question 66 that it is not true that the radio broadcast appeals calling on wealthy Muslims and intellectuals to surrender. The reality is, Mr. Orlovic, members of the non-Serb populations were forced to make statements over the Sana radio calling on other non-Serbs to surrender; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I know that Muslims came to Radio Sanski Most telling people to surrender, and I asked them whether they had been compelled to do it, coerced, and when they told me they had not been, and I told them then, If there is any kind of coercion involved, I don't want you to do this. One of them read it so nicely that I, as a professional, was in awe. I, myself, would have read it much -- much worse, but he who was not a professional read it so beautifully --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's hear the Sanski Most radio broadcast. A prominent Muslim, Faik Biscevic, was forced to make a public statement for the interest of the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is P725. And the portion you will hear starts English page 5, B/C/S page 9 of the transcript. And I think, Mr. President, we can play this without translation because we have translation in Sanction. And I note for the record that the portion -- this portion starts at 1 -- 11 minutes and goes through 11 minutes, 55 seconds of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We paused at 11 minutes -- we paused at 11 minutes and 55 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Orlovic, this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, in terms of transcript what's the page number? Page 5 in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It starts from page 5 in English, B/C/S page 9, and goes over to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Orlovic, this was Mr. Biscevic stating that Sanski Most is a Serb town and warning that Sanski Most could be destroyed until final capitulation. This was the message Radio Sana broadcast to which you refer in answer to question 55 regarding disarming, that unless all weapons were handed over by the Muslims and Croats they would be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, are you dealing with question 66 or 55?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Fifty-five, Mr. President, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And page -- yes, you refer to 66. But okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So this was the kind of message that was broadcast on the radio; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said a moment ago I did not want to name the man but you did so, Faik Biscevic. I asked him two or three times, If you are doing this under coercion, under duress, tell me, I will find a way. But he told me, I am doing this out of my own free will. I don't know if he was lying, but I was surprised at how well he read it, without a single mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Well, let's hear one more portion of this same announcement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This portion starts at 12 minutes, 35 seconds, through 14 minutes and 35 seconds of the tape, and I think we don't need translation because we can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: For the transcript, it should be -- it's the same as previous, sorry. So it starts English page 5, goes 6 and 7; and then B/C/S page 9, goes to 10 and 11. And this should be -- so this portion should be English page 6, B/C/S page 10 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Orlovic, it is not correct, is it, that the radio did not broadcast appeals calling on prominent Muslims to surrender? We just heard exactly that; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was this interlocutor. As for Radio Sanski Most, I mean, no information was provided from some Crisis Staff or someone else for someone to surrender. Quite simply, this is what the interlocutor said -- or rather, the man who came and said that. And Radio Sanski Most did not have any information to that effect about prominent Muslims and Croats. I know many more prominent Muslims and Croats than the one referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In response to question 34 and 68, you say that wartime poverty and personal insecurity drove people to find refuge with people of their own kind. The reality is, however, that the Sana radio, Mr. Orlovic, was used by the Crisis Staff to make it clear to Muslims and Croats that they should leave; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Well, let's hear a radio broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is P725. The portion we will hear starts at English page 2, B/C/S page 2 of the transcript - I think we don't need translation - and this portion starts 2 minutes, 42 seconds, through 5 minutes and 2 seconds of the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we go along with this practice, but it's very difficult to review the testimony of this witness later on. When we read the transcript, we hear in transcript -- we have no idea what part of the transcript was read out because we do not understand the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That I understand, Mr. President. So we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I'm not -- yes, but I will leave it to you, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In that case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In that case, then translators can translate as the tape goes. And as I said, this is English page 2, B/C/S page 2 of the transcript, and we have provided the transcript to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I don't hear a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we don't hear any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English booth now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, shall we repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "An announcement, or rather an appeal, Muslim and Croatian citizens of Sanski Most municipality, you must be aware of the trouble you have been pushed into by the policies of your irresponsible leaders who keep calling for suicidal combat operations which, in these parts, would spell self-destruction for you. Any, half-way rational person realises that propelling your people towards destruction is a crime against your own people in which the innocent would also suffer. In order to achieve some sort of unrealistic and incomprehensible goals in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic chose a war to the death of his own people as a way out of the political cul-de-sac into which he pushed young men, your children, who do not realise what kind of politics they are getting killed for. This policy of his and the activities of his extremist followers have been defeated in our municipality and have no chance of success. You are aware of the results of these crazed and suicidal activities. Because of the unenviable position that your leaders have put you in and because of the great interethnic divide which was not wanted but is present, we deem it reasonable to overcome these problems by asking you to organise your life in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina or another republic of the former Yugoslavia where there would be no interethnic division in order for all the three peoples to feel safe and secure in their areas. It is our opinion that every people should live where it will not only support but also assist the authorities. If the political and legal system in these parts does not suit you, it is necessary for everyone's sake that you organise your life in areas easier for you. The Sanski Most authorities will not only make it possible for you to move safely and freely but will also assist you in the process. Again, we appeal to you to move to a state you would undoubtedly be loyal to, which would normalise life in these parts since living with mutual hatred and interethnic trust is impossible. We expect that you will understand this appeal since this solution is the most painless and that you will respond to our call which we will send out in good time. The Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We discussed earlier the killings and persecutions to which non-Serbs were subjected. We just heard the Crisis Staff publicly informing Croats and Muslims that it is in their best interest to leave, as they risk self-destruction in which the innocent will suffer. So it is not true, is it, that non-Serbs left for economic reasons. They left because it was made clear to them that Sanski Most is a Serb town in which their survival was in jeopardy; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here, "If you do not accept the system or the way it functions ..." so if they wish -- you've forgotten that. You've forgotten to emphasise that. As for the departure of Muslims and Croats, it started considerably before the conflict in Sanski Most, near the bus station. And five months before that, I saw buses every day, especially on Saturdays and Sundays and holidays. They went abroad. It was mainly women and children that went abroad and this caused some fear amongst us, the Serbs. Why wouldn't we go, too? When the war started -- well, it is the right of people to seek shelter from the war and it is also their duty. It's better for people to save their lives rather than to expose themselves to risk. What I need to point out in particular is that during the war in Sanski Most, there were several thousand Muslims who lived there. And today in Sanski Most, out of 28.000 Serbs only about 1.500 are left, and that information is certainly not correct either. So you can make this small comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orlovic, can you just tell us about that newspaper. Did you work there as an editor where your interviews or texts were published?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not work as an editor, and I can say that during the war I was not an editor in Radio Sanski Most at all. I was an ordinary journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In these newspapers, who prepares the headlines, the subheadings? And is that sent to you for pre-authorisation before it is actually published?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is done by the editor or the duty editor, and my texts were not sent back to me for authorisation, so I cannot accept all the texts that I published from 1991 to 1995, especially the radio texts that were cut up in all sorts of ways. All sorts of things were done to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Between pages 8 and 10, what was quoted to you was that you mentioned the spectre of the Ustasha danger or something like that. What led you to refer to that, the spectre of the Ustasha danger?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sanski Most is a special place. I said that five and a half thousand Serbs and Jews were killed in 1941.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please speak slowly. We will finish before the break.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Viktor Gutic, in 1941, stated in Sanski Most, "The Serbs will be missed, but there won't be any left." Every Serb in the territory of Sanski Most remembered that and it reverberates in a very bad way. So Sanski Most is left without Serbs, after all. And there are many things that can be said in this regard. I don't think that we can deal with it all now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what happened, what policy was promoted in neighbouring Croatia? And how far away is that from you? How far away is the Croatian border?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian border is not far away from Sanski Most, up to 80 kilometres, and it's even less as the crow flies. There were many Serbs who lived in Croatia and then after the conflict in Croatia they came to Sanski Most. Entire columns of refugees came and the people of Sanski Most saw them coming, they told them about terrible things that had happened, and that fuelled the fear that something like that could happen to them, too. The war in Croatia was really a special phenomenon, something that led to this psychosis among the population in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I kindly ask you, Mr. Orlovic, to relax, to sit down properly, and speak slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, it's what a journalist does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Certain things were mentioned here that were broadcast over the radio. Did you write a statement to this Mr. Biscevic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. Mr. Biscevic brought this statement. It was in his pocket. Again, I repeat: I asked him not to read it out, even if he was under pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The objection raised to you was that the radio broadcast statements of the Crisis Staff. Did you write these statements, and did you have the right not to air them?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not write the statements that we received. We broadcast them in the original and we did not have the right to change them for a simple reason: That is what we had been told, that the original should be left as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the names that were mentioned, Savic and Biscevic's statement, and the names that he mentions saying that he is expressing their views, too, that the fighting should stop? And the Prosecutor has suggested that these were prominent Muslims. Are these the names of people -- actually, who are these people in terms of political activity?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, these people were then members of the Party of Democratic Action. I repeat once again, I knew a lot of prominent Muslims who were in the fields of science, arts, and who were professors, and of course he doesn't mention them, and they were probably more eminent than they were. I am not going into that now. I'm not going to weigh their respective reputations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the position of those that he did not mention and where did they live?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They lived -- they lived in Sanski Most. They lived in their apartments. In my building, an engineer lived there, a professor, and throughout these different activities we were together in the hallway. We played chess, we took care of each other. And we trembled. I trembled as much as he did. I was afraid for my children but he did not have to fear for his children because he had sent them away several months before that, so he was more aware of the situation that would actually happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown D5, Defence exhibit number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this, the State Security Service, the 7th of March, 1992. And it says: "According to verified information, certain persons wearing ... Green Berets were observed," and so on and so forth. And it also says according to realistic estimates, about 3.000 Muslims owned long-barrels and are part of the SDA armed formation and those mainly responsible for the SDA activities are Ismet Sarcevic, a lawyer; Suad Sabic, a lawyer; Adil Draganovic, president of the court; Redzo Kurbegovic; and Mirzet Karabeg; and Enver Hurlic, commander of the police station. How does this fit into what you know, this information of the state security before the war?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I lived a peaceful life. I didn't really meddle into politics. Different stories were bandied about, about arming, and we were all in fear of each other. The Muslims were saying that we were armed and we were saying that they were armed. Again, I didn't really believe it that much; however, when I read the book: "It is a Crime To Forget a Crime," I saw that on the 15th of April there was this review, this lineup of 300 armed persons in Vrhpolje. Later on when there was this disarming - the radio is near the bus station - I saw in cars lots of different weapons, the old guns that were used for celebratory gun-fire, but also I saw the most sophisticated modern weapons. So there were weapons there. Now how they obtained weapons, there are several versions in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that book that you mention, who are the authors of that book?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zilhad Kljucanin and I forgot the naming of the other author. Akmadzic? Now, what was his name? You'll probably find it somewhere. Roughly it was only then that we saw what the actual situation was on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what their ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Muslims, and I know Kljucanin well because he was a poet like I am. He wrote poetry and lived in Sarajevo for a while and then returned to Sanski Most. And then he went back to Sarajevo. He divided his time between these two towns and he is a highly educated man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 51 of that book, I don't know whether that part is there, it says certain quantities of weapons were obtained from Croatia. One of the main organisers of the purchase of weapons in the municipality of Sanski Most was Hasim Kamber [phoen], at that time secret of the SDA, together with Rasim. That is page 52. The next one, Karabeg, Karabeg, Kamir [phoen], managed to obtain some explosives towards the end of 1991 and beginning of 1992. And now there is a list of persons who worked on obtaining weapons: Seferovic, Begic Sudo, Redzo Kurbegovic, Suad Sabic, Enver Hurlic, Nedzad Muhic, Faik Biscevic, Mirzet Karabeg, Husein Efendija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not following.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It's kind of reading session. I don't understand, what was the question? I think Mr. Karadzic asked and he got the answer on this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now I'm asking the witness what his knowledge was about this, about what the Muslim authors were saying about these prominent people, as they were called by the Prosecutor in his question. All of these persons are being mentioned as organisers of illegal arming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Where do we have that quote?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, it's not this document. It's the book that we showed a moment ago. I don't know whether these pages have been admitted. They have already been admitted, I see. I just need to find out what the number is because the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- did not show all documents. He just made certain references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Karadzic asked this question about arming and he got the answer from the witness. I don't understand why he needs to feed the witness more about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you assist us, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't think there is anything wrong with supporting the witness's answer by showing other documents or corroborating the witness by showing him other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, he can do that as long as he's not leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I see I won't be able to finish before the break, after all, so perhaps we should take the break. D1677, that's the number. This Muslim book -- or rather, this book by Muslim authors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. President, I wanted to address the issue you left with the parties in light of the impossibility of extended sessions, you noted at the outset that you would leave to the parties how to proceed. Mr. Robinson and I consulted by e-mail on this issue. We would suggest, if the Court and personnel are amenable, having 20-minute breaks instead of 30 minutes and having a 30-minute lunch which would yield an additional 50 minutes and might enable us to complete the process. I appreciate that's a burden. I wouldn't ordinarily suggest it, but it is an expedient that just might serve our purposes under these circumstances as a rare exception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, how much longer would you need for your re-examination to be concluded?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We shall first take a break for 20 minutes and resume at 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to let the parties know that it has been arranged that the Chamber can sit till 10 past 4.00 today. Please, Mr. Karadzic, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orlovic, we have seen what the radio broadcast, and I don't know if we got an answer to this question. Were you able to change the announcements of the authorities?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not able to and they were published -- they were broadcast in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the municipality of Sanski Most, were there any villages that handed over their weapons; Serb, Muslim, and Croat?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a number of villages that handed over their weapons and continued to live peacefully. A friend of mine from the village of Kijevo, when he found out that there would be a disarmament drive, asked me what to do and I told him, Advise your people over there to hand over their weapons, and you'll surely be able to go on living peacefully. Later on he called me to say that everything was all right. So that was Kijevo village. Another one was Poljak. And some other villages that I knew about, because friends of mine called me from there and said that things were quite peaceful in those villages after they handed over their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the total number of Muslim and Croat villages in Sanski Most municipality, and in how many of them was there any fighting?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but I'll probably not be wrong if I say around 50. And out of that, half were Muslim, half were Serb, and perhaps there were two or three Croat villages. I'm not really sure but something like that. Disarmament drives and incidents took place in a number of villages. We've managed to refer already to Mahala, Hrustovo, and there was an incident in Trnava village where the police was disarmed. And in the immediate vicinity, a soldier who was guarding a silo was killed. There were some incidents in these places and I don't remember any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier today the Prosecutor questioned your claim that communications were interrupted, and he also suggested that attacks on Mahala and some other villages targeted civilian settlements and you claim the opposite.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show 65 ter 8463 to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Perhaps we should first hear the question and then see the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orlovic, do you stand by your assertion that the fighting did not target unarmed civilian settlements as the Prosecutor claimed?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by that assertion based on the knowledge that I had, and I had that knowledge from the reports that were sent to us at the radio for us to broadcast them, where people of good intentions who did not want conflict who were prepared to hand over weapons would be safe if they do so. In places where clashes occurred, they occurred probably because they didn't want to hand over weapons or there were skirmishes between individuals who were out of control with groups or individuals from another ethnic community.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we have the document on the screen, could we show page 10 in Serbian and then we'll move on to page 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this 8467 -- 63?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This should be 1677. It's already in evidence. We'll leave it. Let's have 8463. This has already been received. I only wanted to show on the screen what I've already read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orlovic, we should also have the English version. We have one report from the news agency "Tanjug." We see the date 27 July and something in handwriting. Look at the last paragraph. "Due to the complete breakdown of PTT communications ... with municipalities Sanski Most and Kljuc, we have no other details on today's clashes." How is this consistent with your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: PTT communications were frequently broken down, especially after various operations, and I believe the most critical months were May and June where PTT communications operated very badly or not at all. We had local communications in certain areas but not outside the borders of the municipality -- or only sporadically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the rest, please. It deals with the conflict between Muslim extremists and the units of the 1st Krajina Corps. It says they broke out today at Sanski Most. And the previous night an attack at guards in Venicevci [phoen] village and Vrhpolje village, these guards were guarding the bridge on the Sana River. And it says that Green Berets fired mortars at the public security station and the silo. How is this consistent with what you know?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, there was frequent shooting. Since I didn't serve in the army, I don't really distinguish between shells and mortars. Shells did fall in and around the place where I lived. I don't know from where. But where I lived there was only Serbian population, and at the Radio Sanski Most when the shells were falling there were only Serbs inside. Only Serbs working there. So I suppose these shells were fired by the other side because that radio was the only mass medium that was still operating and could inform the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that these shells destroyed a number of houses in that Serbian settlement?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did know a couple of things. I remember one shell fell very near me. I know. But at that time, people did not really count damaged houses. What was important was to get out of it alive. Whether something would be destroyed or not was less important, so we didn't really count any material damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the last paragraph. Tell us if it fits in with your experience. Was the deputy commander of the police killed in an ambush, and did a clash occur between the police and the locals who were joined by people from Velagici village? This is not Sanski Most municipality, but did you know about these things?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not then, but information reached us later. Both information and disinformation reached us later. But much later I found out there had been some incidents and a group of soldiers were killed when they were going from Kljuc. Those were JNA soldiers who were going back. At that time in that period, and we've shown recently this book, "It's A Crime to Forget a Crime," on the 15th of April in Vrhpolje there was a lineup of 300 armed men. So these things could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be useful that we have some information about the "Tanjug," where this -- what this agency is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, for the record. Yes. It -- could you assist us, Mr. Orlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking me about the "Tanjug" report? I see it for the first time. I was not aware of it. But they probably got it from a source.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orlovic, for the record, just tell us what "Tanjug" is.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the telegraph news agency of Yugoslavia, created back in the Second World War, and it was based in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4295, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Prosecution suggested that Mahala and several other settlements were attacked as civilian settlements. Do you still stand by your assertion that these settlements were militarised, that they had a military organisation?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these settlements from what we knew from the information that reached us through various reports at the radio, and from what we heard from people, from what I heard, a large number of people had weapons. And that was proven later during the disarmament drives. And wherever there are weapons, there is danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were civilians the target of the Serbian Territorial Defence and later the 6th Sana Brigade, and still later the Army of Republika Srpska? Were you able to see for yourself whether civilians were the target?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what Radio Sanski Most broadcast, and these were constant announcements and reports, the population of these settlements had previously been asked to leave the place to avoid civilian casualties. These announcements were broadcast minute by minute and the aim was to keep the civilian population, women, children, and all those people who were unarmed and unwilling to join in the fighting, safe. They were asked to leave. I saw a column of people from my window in the radio building cross a bridge and go into the premises of the football club Podgrmec. They were escorted by the police and I believe they made their way in peace.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 65 ter 18911.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Orlovic, read to us slowly the first paragraph of item 1. First tell the Trial Chamber who published this, who is this person, and what is this?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the combat assignment to disarm people in Sanski Most, Prijedor, 1, 2, 3, and 4, Bosanska Krupa. I don't see the signature of the person. Colonel Anicic, commander of the Territorial Defence Staff. Colonel, but I can't see the name, it seems to be Anicic. I'm reading the text: "In certain parts of the municipality populated by Muslims and Croats, some earlier infiltrated groups like HOS," which is probably Croatian Armed Forces, "ZNG, and Green Berets linked up with the forces of hostile villages and urban neighbourhoods of Sanski Most municipality, and with their help managed to establish eight detachments, five independent companies, and several independent platoons in Mahala, Kamengradska Balina [phoen], Hrustovo, Vrhpolje, Trnovo, Sehovici, Sasina and Poljak. Onto the free territory of the city and environs, the enemy intensively infiltrating individuals who have intelligence, reconnaissance, and sabotage assignments."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This was the end of the sight translation. Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Interpreters were able to translate the citation but not your question. So if you could repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How does this report issued by the commander of the Territorial Defence Staff tally with what you knew about those eight detachments, five independent companies in those locations that are mentioned, Mahala, Hrustovo, and Vrhpolje, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were rumours about some detachments and companies and about ZNGs and HOS troops having been infiltrated. I didn't know how many there were. This is the first time I see that they were so numerous. If I had known it at the time, I would have run for my life. This is an impressive force, I dare say. In other words, the situation was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orlovic, what does it say in the right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Strictly confidential, Grmec 1992," which is probably a code.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this perhaps the reason why you were not aware of the details?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. Because if this information had become public, I'm sure that it would have instilled a lot of panic among the people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we go to the following page --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think this document might be in evidence already. And second, this witness testified that he doesn't know anything about these activities. All he knew was what he was receiving on the radio. I don't see the point going on this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to defer to Dr. Karadzic as to whether this is a good use of our time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, the Prosecutor challenged the fact that it was combat and legitimate action. He claimed that there were attacks on demilitarised Muslim and Croat villages and urban areas. The witness said that that was not the fact. And now I would like to show a confidential document which had to be kept secret in order to prevent panic among the population in order to establish who is right, whether it's the witness or Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably I think it would -- I agree that I saw this document before. Do you know the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'm trying to locate it, Mr. President, as I -- if I manage, I'll let you know. And second, this witness testified he does not know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably Mr. Karadzic wanted to tender this document. But if this is the one we have already admitted, that's a -- he should consider again whether it's a good use of time given that the witness cannot help us a lot as to the content of this document.
