We certainly discussed with Mr. Keserovic. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It might be P3313, but it need to cross-check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's confirmed by the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me give you the reason. On page 22, the question was: [In English] "You say in response to question 12 that after Mahala, Muslim extremists who did not want to surrender weapons withdrew to Caplje and Hrustovo where the fighting with them continued. Mr. Orlovic, while you claim this happened, you reported to the Serb mass media ...," and so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I confirm this was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orlovic, on page 21 and also on page 22, and I'm going to read the question: [In English] "And you knew, Mr. Orlovic, that ordinary civilians were killed in Sanski Most, didn't you?" And answer: "At that time there was a lot of rumor, a lot of propaganda. All the stories including murders, killings, and destruction, I always took them with a grain of salt. I never believed them. Even 20 years after the end of the war, I still don't believe that things like that happened. All the cases that did occur, they cannot be seen as falling under the system or part of some organised activity. Those were individual incidents that should be condemned." [Interpretation] Do you adhere by this, Mr. Orlovic? According to what you know, how did authorities -- how did the authorities view such incidents?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I adhere to my words. As far as the authorities are concerned, at that moment the authorities were dealing with the situation at hand. I believe that all those incidents would eventually be prosecuted and that the perpetrators of those illegal acts would eventually be punished and that they would be taken to task for what they had done.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 65 ter 6734.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was issued on the 10 November 1992 by the public security station. It was signed by its chief, Mirko Vrucinic, as you will see on the last page. In the first paragraph it says: "In the last month or so, violence against settlements and persons of Muslim and Croat nationality in the area of Sanski Most municipality has escalated." The text goes on to list all the incidents that happened and the dates when they happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The second sentence in the second paragraph says that the perpetrators of those acts are mostly members of military and paramilitary and most of them enjoy support of the other soldiers, and some representatives of the authorities which believe that the official authorities had not done enough to move Muslims and Croats out of the territory of the municipality. Most of those acts were in retaliation, and so on and so forth. What about this position of the police? How does that tally with what you know and what you experienced with regard to the position of the authorities in connection with crimes?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was still the early days of the war. It was a hot year, as it were. There were a lot of activities going on. First of all, the corridor of life was created, then there were actions around Jajce. From all of those places, we heard that people died in large numbers or they returned wounded. This created an anxiety among the people who were sent to the front line. All those things were individual things. They were not part of a system. Nobody actually ordered them to do what they did. They were either drunk when they did what they did or they were sick. God knows. In any case, they had their own reasons why they did those things, and if one is to judge by Mr. Vrucinic's words, the police was ready to punish the perpetrators of those acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please pay attention to the follow passage where it says: "We inform you that in all instances SJB operatives performed on-site investigations and undertook legal measures and acts, and that at this moment we know who some of the perpetrators are. However, ... in a situation like this, we neither can, nor is it advisable to undertake measures of arresting," and so on and so forth. Please take a look at this passage. It says here that there is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- a fear that certain soldiers will not allow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow, Mr. Karadzic. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is the same: How does this tally with Mr. Orlovic's conviction that the police did prosecute such acts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- ex officio.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How does he know that, first? And then second, how does this arise from the cross-examination, the investigation or something? Did Mr. Zec touch upon that issue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on pages 21 and 22. The question was: [In English] "And you knew, Mr. Orlovic, that ordinary civilians were killed in Sanski Most; didn't you?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, he didn't touch upon the issue of investigation or the prosecution, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Excellencies, the witness answered that there were such things but that they were not part of a system. They were not condoned by the authorities. And I want to see from him whether the authorities undertook measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zec is certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4296, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now the last document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know, Mr. Orlovic, how the authorities looked at those things? What did they expect from members of the armed forces when it came to illegal acts and crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I believe this goes -- same topic. There is nothing different from the previous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I would like to show the witness my last document and then I'll wrap it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. If it is related to this topic, I will not allow you to go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's about the protection of all citizens --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- regardless of their religion or ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ask your question first. We'll hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to give you a reference from the cross-examination. Mr. Orlovic -- please bear with me for a moment. The page number is 30 and the question was this: [In English] "We discussed earlier that killings and persecution to which non-Serbs were subjected. We just heard the Crisis Staff publicly informing Croats and Muslims that it is in their best interest to leave, as they risk self-destruction in which the innocent will suffer. So it is not true, is it, that non-Serbs left more economic reasons. They left because it was made clear that Sanski Most is a Serb town in which their survival was in jeopardy; right?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: non-Serbs, non-Serbian civilians, the non-Serb population as is suggested by this question?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I received from the police station and the authorities, i.e., the information we received after their meetings, there were no such things. There was never a reference made to the need to persecute non-Serbs. All effort was made to protect them. But it was wartime. Laws were not implemented in the way they should have been. There were a lot of disappointed people who had weapons and who could not be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now the last document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that I would like to call up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note Mr. Zec referred to "persecution," but he never mentioned "prosecution."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Persecution. [Interpretation] Persecution. I never said "prosecution." I mentioned [indiscernible] or "persecution." I wanted to see whether the authorities persecuted non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 5172 is the next document I would like to call up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your 15 minutes turned out to be almost an hour. I do not interrupt -- stopping you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, had Mr. Zec not interrupted it would have been less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orlovic, please take a look at this. Between two sessions of the assembly, the co-ordination body reached a decision or, rather, decisions. We can all read this out. Just take a look at the first two. Does this support an assertion to the effect that the authorities were in favour of persecuting civilians?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of these conclusions, no, because it can be seen, after all, that it is responsibility that is being required.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What conclusion are we talking about, Mr. Orlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the command is -- I mean the first one, the first conclusion: "The commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade and the Public Security Station are requested to submit a report on who participated in the organisation of the armed attack on Trnovo and Sehovici and what was the goal of an attack on such a scale." So a report is being requested and probably they are being held responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, so the 6th Krajina Brigade and the public security station are required to do what? The most strict possible measures should be taken, they should change certain personnel. How does this fit into what you said, that the authorities did not persecute civilians and the prosecutor is saying that they did?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't fit into that because the authorities started to function. This is the 17th of November when these conclusions were adopted, so it is already in sight; namely, those who perpetrated crimes would be held accountable. So that means that, after all, the situation in the municipality is calming down and there is more freedom of movement and life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What does this attack on Trnovo and Sehovici refer to? Do you remember that, Mr. Orlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The attack against Trnovo and Sehovici probably refers to -- well, according to my knowledge, according to what I knew, in Trnovo the police had been disarmed and they say that they stripped them naked and expelled them from the village. And in Sehovici there was a silo nearby where a soldier had been killed who had been guarding the grains there and probably there was some clash after the activity of the extremists in these villages. That was probably the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They were the attacks against the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, whatever you call it, attacks, excesses. Policemen were there probably with the task of protecting the village but they were attacked. The soldier who was guarding the grains probably had no other intention but to guard the grains.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Orlovic, you say that that was probably the reason or taken as a pretext for something. What is it that the authorities hold against the armed elements? So it was a pretext for what?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably for what happened in those villages, Trnovo and Sehovici. I know of these situations, these things that happened in these villages. But I know that in this village of Sehovici there is a large Roma population. They were loyal throughout the war and nobody touched them. I know that they came to see me at the radio. They would ask for certain songs to be played. They expressed their wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, in the previous document of the 10th of November it says -- I mean, these villages are referred to where these incidents occurred against the Muslims and Croats. And here --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- a week --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The -- this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic is explaining the relevance of this document in order to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And witness provided it so far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: -- and Mr. Karadzic is moving on. He is referring to other document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, he concluded his re-examination. He's explaining to the Chamber as to the relevance and admissibility of this document. I will turn to you. Please wait. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These two documents are a linked to the previous one of the 10th of November where these incidents are enumerated. The witness said that the reasons or pretext for these incidents were some murders, but the authorities believed that this was too much. And this has been admitted but under a different number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zec. Any objection to the admission of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: My also concern was, as Your Honours already asked the witness about, this relates to specificities, incidents, and the witness provided the answer so I don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4297, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless my colleagues have further questions for you, Mr. Orlovic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session. The Chamber will rise for three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll rise for ten minutes for preparation. --- Break taken at 11.45 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the remainder of today's session, we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis with Judge Baird being away due to his personal urgent matters. Before we continue, could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Witness, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the international Tribunal; that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the witness please be shown, without broadcasting this, 8804. That's the 65 ter number. I'm sorry, 1D8804. This can be removed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, do you see this page before you and does this number correspond to your name?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: My name is written down there, but I don't know about these numbers up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this is your name on this sheet?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4298 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you provide a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for pausing between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 1D9659, again without having it broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the first page of that statement of yours on the screen?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page so that he could identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I would like to ask you to pause between our questions and answers. Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this statement faithfully reflect what you communicated to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today in this courtroom, would your answers basically be the same as those contained in the statement?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement on the basis of Rule 92 ter under seal, and could you please decide on a possible redacted version for the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to the statement, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive both versions, i.e., a confidential version as well as public version, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 1D9659 will be Exhibit D4299 under seal, and the public redacted version will be Exhibit D4300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we deal with the associate exhibits? I -- yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There are two proposed associated exhibits. They are not on our 65 ter list as we hadn't interviewed this witness at the time that this was filed. With respect to the second one, it's actually part of paragraph 13 and not paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Second one being 1D9653?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. With respect to that folder, which consists of six photos, no explanation is offered as to who those other individuals are, so probably that needs to be led live. But we'll receive 1D9658 unless there is any objection from Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we assign a number for the first one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4301 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read out in the English language a summary of this witness's statement, and then I'm going to put a few questions to him and also deal with a few documents live. [In English] KW426 worked in the RS State Security Service. He became a communications and encoding instructor and during his career he was also responsible for training and defence preparations. He is not affiliated to any political party. The ethnic composition of the CSB where he worked was, for the most part, unchanged before and after the war and all ethnic groups were equally represented. When the war broke out in BH, there was no direct communication with the organs at the republican level for a while. The vertical line of subordination to the republican authorities was severed due to physical cutting off of the territory and disruption of the communication lines. The CSB where this witness worked, special police unit, was formed in April 1992 pursuant to the decision of the assembly of the regional organisation. The unit had three army platoons and one police platoon. Almost no one in the special unit had specialist training. In mid-July 1992, the Ministry of the Interior issued an order to disband the unit. In addition, about 40 men were removed from the unit for disciplinary reasons and criminal reports were filed against a number of them. After this experience, it was decided that only educated and trained men could be employed at the CSB. During the war, most members of the special police unit were conscientious and responsible men, who did not commit crimes. With regard to the Keraterm and Omarska investigation centre, the CSB where this witness worked appointed a commission which was supposed to establish whether there were any irregularities in the work of these centres. The commission produced a report which was accepted as credible and accurate and in which it was said that various paramilitary formations committed crimes in the centres and that the police was unable to oppose them. Steps were taken to overcome the crisis situation and disband and disarm all paramilitary formations. And that is short summary. I would like now to pose several questions and show some documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just one advice to the witness before he starts his evidence. Because your voice should be distorted for the purpose of protection, please make sure that you put a pause between the question and answer before you start answering the question. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you overlap with the interpretation, your voice might be heard outside. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you need some kind of orientation, Witness, you can see whether my light is on or not. Once it's off, it is safe for you to start speaking. Can you tell us whether you had information about any paramilitary or illegal organisation of the other two sides in your area and when that started?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Well according to the information that I have, paramilitary formations in the area of the centre of Banja Luka were established already during the election campaign. I know that from some notes. After certain things happened -- actually, after these elections, part of the weapons and equipment were hidden in bunkers, houses, and later on some of the owners of these houses, because they left some other valuables there, in a way they tried to get this out illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D9654. And I believe that it can be broadcast, but first let us take a look at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is and how you got it? If you're the only person who managed to get ahold of it, it cannot be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: This document was captured when a command post was being taken, a command post of the BH Army. And persons that took part in fighting were familiar with this document. These are the unit cards of that unit that remained at the command post, and this shows that certain soldiers had joined the unit already in 1990; that is to say, before anything happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this one joined?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: On the 25th of September, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or maybe it's the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about this soldier? When did he --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, Excellencies, you decide whether this can be broadcast. I think it can be broadcast. It has nothing to do with the identity of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be broadcast. Could it please be broadcast, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you look at this card, what do you see? When did this person join the armed forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: According to this card, on -- in April 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is written next to this rank in the former JNA? What does it say there?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Squad leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What does it say on the next page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this person joined? Just please pause. When this person joined the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: The 23rd of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please leaf through this one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And without me putting any questions, could you just tell us when every one of these persons became a member of the armed forces. And then I'm going to put questions to you after that. So I'm going to turn off my microphone now, and then you tell us about all the rest. Just tell me when this person joined their illegal army.

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: August 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please leaf through all of them for the witness with short breaks so that he could identify this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st of January 1992; March 1992; 15th of March, 1992; the 2nd of April, 1992; the 4th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Can you tell us how things stood in relation to the law? As far as these cards are concerned, what was the legal armed force at the time according to the law?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: According to the law this was illegal activity because at that point in time, no such military formation was supposed to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I mean, this is untranslated material, but I am nevertheless struggling to see the relevance. Obviously, it's not contested whatsoever that there was an army, the ABiH, with soldiers. I understand that this is an effort to show that there was some kind of organisation of some armed units in 1990 and 1991; however, we have no idea where such units were formed or anything about any particulars and how it made impacts on any of the municipalities or allegations in this case. I'm happy to have it MFI'd for the time being. But again, I'm unclear as to the relevance of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification, pending English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4302, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, may I ask you to tell us briefly, but still in greater detail, what these units were, where they were deployed, and what their purpose was?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: This is a purely military unit. I'd like to emphasise that I saw similar cards in Doboj when I went there on official business. A colleague of mine showed them to me at an SDA station. They had similar cards in cardboard boxes and they were labeled: "The Distribution of Military Scripts Across Jenac [phoen]," which were religious institutions. And that is an indication that in that area as well this military force had already been prepared, which was illegal because all military formations and all military conscripts were under the department for national defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The indictment against me alleges that Muslims and Croats were dismissed from our services and that it was made impossible for them to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I don't think it's appropriate to introduce a question by reciting allegations in the indictment, particularly when the indictment actually doesn't make any such allegations. At least not with this kind of specificity. But in any event, it's just -- it's just leading to do it this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably by "indictment" he might have included your pre-trial brief. But could you explain why making reference to the indictment and pre-trial brief is leading in its nature?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, it's just providing the witness with information as to how his answer might impact on the accused's guilt or innocence, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it's -- can he not ask whether an allegation in the indictment is true or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, he can just ask the question without --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Without saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you rose when he was reading out -- making reference to the indictment, "Alleges that Muslims and Croats were dismissed from our service and that it was impossible for them to work," and that's the moment you stood up.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I -- I maintained that in my position that it's leading because it tells the witness how his answer to a question might impact on the accused's guilt or innocence to the charges, and in that respect I think it's leading and I see no need. If he can -- he can just ask questions about whether Muslims or Croats were dismissed from certain positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you are asking -- the Prosecution is asking a question to the witness, you make references to a lot of exhibit numbers. So it's just for the Chamber to follow and for the cross-reference. I don't see any problem with it. But, Mr. Robinson, could you assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think it would be a lot of assistance if the Prosecution would wait until they hear the questions before they make objections. This is a pattern and I'm sure they wouldn't appreciate it if we did that in the course of their cross-examination anticipating what we think the question is going to be. So I think we would all be better served if they would simply just wait until the question is put. If there is an objection, to put it at this time. This seems to be a pattern that is not helpful to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. If I could just reply. It's largely for technical reasons that we have to stand as soon as possible because otherwise, because of the -- the fact that this is all going on in B/C/S, the witness usually starts the answer before we get a chance to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, in the area in the place where you worked - and we've heard it had something to do with security - in the service where you worked, how would you qualify it from the perspective of security, national security? Was it a sensitive place?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: It was a very important security service, and we had certain obligations stipulated by the law. In this initial period, the service was depoliticised. The service was made up of professionals. We were not members of any political party, and we were supposed to serve all national groups within the country. In that period when strife began at the political level, in my own centre people of all ethnicities continued to work. And I can say that because I, as an operator of equipment, in end 1990 distributed to all active duty and reserve employees of the service a certain amount of weapons and ammunition, and the same was done when the president of the republic died. In this emergency situation, it was decided that employees of the security service should be armed. And they were armed regardless of ethnicity. There is documentation about that. And we made quarterly reports about our levels of equipment, and we can see from these lists that out of 68 employees, there was 27 Muslims and Croats who also received weapons, official IDs, and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, could you just clarify when the president of the republic died? Which president do you mean and which time was it when you distributed weapons?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: That was when the president of Yugoslavia, Josip Bros Tito, died. I was then employed with the service and I know these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in which period did these 27 Croats and Muslims work in your unit?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Both before and after. I believe there is documentation; for instance, a security provided to the mission to the United Nations and -- of the United Nations and the EU was provided by Muslims and Serbs together. We can see from the notes that they wrote and the records they made, they did it jointly because a decision had been made to make up mixed teams. And that's how it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say before and after, are you talking about the death of President Tito or after what? Which time are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: My last answer referred to the teams guarding Hotel Bosna. They provided security to international delegations who came to attend the funeral. And I also talked about teams that participated in peace efforts between HVO, the Croatian forces, and the Serb forces. They participated on an equal footing in these missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When the war broke out, did these representatives of other ethnic communities in your agencies continue to work or were they dismissed?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: They continued to work. I know some of them personally who are still in the police force and in the top security agency.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D9655 is the document I'd like to call up next. It should not be broadcast because it could identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what is this document?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: This is the duty service log-book of the mission providing security to ECMM, European monitors, and you can see all the people who served as guards. And you can see that alongside Serbs there were Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This Meho, the ninth person from the top, what is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Two lines below, Hajrudin, what is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Also Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last one, (redacted) Slavko.

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Let me see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we redact the last name, let it be just Slavko. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On this page, would you draw our attention to something in particular?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Under number 3, you have Amir (redacted) It says -- it's misspelled here. The man was "Amor" not "Amir."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Leave out the last names.

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Amor and Zeljko. The first one is a Muslim, the second one is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The third and fourth line from the bottom, are they also a Muslim and a Croat?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. It seems that there are more names listed here of persons whom they were guarding rather than the guards.

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document under seal for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we know the time-frame for this? Yes, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was in 1992. This log-book was created in the beginning of 1992. It was started at the beginning of 1992 and for the duration of the stay of representatives of the UN and EU in Banja Luka. This log-book was kept recording interesting information about their missions into the field, any incidents that might have happened, et cetera, and the same team stayed on this mission, on this job throughout 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure we should put this under seal. Mr. Robinson or Ms. Gustafson? Yeah, we go back to -- go to private session, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe these documents certainly identify me because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Shall we go back to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark this for identification, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4303 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, when did you think we would have our next break? Because so far we had a bit of an unusual schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much more for your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three documents, similar topics. I don't think I'll take long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We shall take a break. We shall have a break for 40 minutes and the resume at 20 past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.41 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in your job did you have an opportunity to examine the work of Merhamet, which was a Muslim humanitarian organisation, and did you co-operate with that organisation?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Yes. I co-operated with Merhamet. I was a liaison officer who actually inspected and communicated with all religious institutions, which means that I had very good relations with all the three religions and organisation which were their integral parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Those three humanitarian organisations that belonged to three different religions, were they treated differently when it came to the performance of their duties? Was any one of them discriminated against?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: As far as I know, none of them was discriminated against. The people resorted to them because there was a shortage of all bare necessities, irrespective of their ethnic affiliation; for example, if Caritas had some humanitarian aid, they would distribute it equally to all religious groups and the same went for the other two religions. There were no divisions along either ethnic or religious lines.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D9657 and the document shouldn't be broadcast. A redacted version can be prepared to become a public version of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us about this document but use as few names as possible.

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: This document was issued by Merhamet, in keeping with the previous agreement, sent a list of the personnel that they needed for humanitarian activities. Those people were to go to Zagreb and back because in Zagreb they had a supply centre where they kept their humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The date is 20th October.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page, please. Again, this shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, it says -- no, the first paragraph: "We have received your letter," so-and-so, "in respect of our request," and so on and so forth, "you inform us about the possibility of assigning military conscripts to work for Merhamet." What would have been the religious affiliation of those conscripts you assigned to work in Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: It was only logical that we assigned Muslims to those duties. At the end of the day, those people would have worked for an organisation that belonged to a -- the Muslim population and Merhamet was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, it says: "We appreciate your willingness to give us a number of people to work in Merhamet to maintain its functions. However, the fact is that those functions cannot be implemented if only the elderly and infirm people are engaged, both women and men, and persons who were born before 1947. In addition to the fact that we have very few staff, we emphasise that we need a certain number of military conscripts who are educated and physically able to perform certain duties." What was the response of your associates and yourself to this request?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: This request was written because they needed personnel. At that time we have -- had a shortage of everything including medicines, toiletries, food stuffs, so it was in our mutual interest to have as much supplies as possible, which is why we met their request. However, this was a normal channel of communication. First everything was agreed, then they sent us a letter, and then we would send them our approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: These Muslim military conscripts, were they duty-bound to respond to mobilisation calls the same as Serbs did?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Yes, they should have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they forced to joint the Army Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: No, nobody was forced to do that. However, those who did not respond to call-ups were considered to be in breach of discipline, so they lost some of their benefits in the companies that they worked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does this mean, they asked for certain age groups or people of certain ages; right?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were their requests met, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: As far as I know, their requests were met.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence, and it should be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why should this -- should this not have been broadcast?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, on the first page there is a name that should not become public. Can we go back to the first page? If this name is redacted and the name of the addressee or just the name, then this version can also become public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4304 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll -- are you going to tender a redacted version, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be MFI D4305.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Excellencies. At this moment, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now in your statement you talked about a lack of communications. You said that when the war broke out, there was no direct communication with the republic for a while. And I believe you're referring to communications from the Banja Luka CSB to the republic level of the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: I was referring to the communications between Krajina where we were and Pale, where the leadership was. The communications channels used were the same for the police and for all the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. During what period of time, specifically, do you claim there were no communications between the Banja Luka CSB and the RS MUP headquarters?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: That happened after the conflicts broke out. The territory was cut off. After 20 years, it's very hard for me to give you the exact time, but I believe that that happened before the corridor was created and even later due to some technical problems. And the communication links did not function as well as they should have.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the evidence in this case is that the corridor was created in late June 1992. So accepting that, would it be your position that from roughly mid-April to late June 1992 there were no communications between the Banja Luka CSB and the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: I can't pin-point the time. What I'm saying is that communications were bad, there were total interruptions at times. There were periods of time when there was no communication at all. If I give you any specific times, I may be wrong. I know that such things did happen, but I really can't tell you when exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Are you aware that the RS MUP produced daily bulletins containing information on security matters, information that was gathered from the CSBs which they had in turn gathered from the SJB in their area? Are you aware of that practice?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I have never seen a bulletin of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So I suppose you're similarly unaware that between mid-April and late June, the RS MUP daily bulletins regularly contained detailed information on security events in municipalities within the Banja Luka CSB area?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Examples would be P2748, 2749, P2791, P2762.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Are you unaware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that [as interpreted]. I know that communications functioned at times. At times they didn't. I don't know for how long. I can't give you any dates. I was not directly involved in communications, so I can't speak about them. I know that often they were interrupted, that there were frequent problems with communications at the republican level.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript. The beginning of the sentence on line 22, the witness said, "I can't confirm that," and the rest of that reply has been properly recorded and this obviously can be reviewed by listening to the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that -- having said that, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said that I could not confirm that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In your previous answer you said you know that there were frequent problems with communications at the republican level, but you also say that you were not directly involved in communications. The Chamber has received evidence from Dragan Kezunovic, who was the chief of communications for the RS MUP, and he testified that although not all of the communication systems worked all the time, there was always some way of communicating. And that's P2743, paragraph 10. I take it you would agree that the chief of communications for the RS MUP is better placed than you to access the quality of communications between the RS MUP and the CSBs during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: I can only give you my observations. I know that at the time the problem existed. Now as to whether the chief of communications was better informed or not, I don't know. I only knew that there were major problems with that and things did happen. How people managed to bridge that gap, whether that was via couriers or in another way, I don't know. And I don't know whether they sent daily reports or whether they sent occasional reports with certain delays. I don't know. Other people did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now at paragraph 4 of your statement, you claim that the ethnic composition of the Banja Luka CSB was, for the most part, unchanged before the war and after it started. And then you list a number of non-Serbs by name who you claim were employees of the security service both before and after the war started. But it's true, is it not, that a number of the people that you specifically mention didn't remain employees of the CSB for very long after the war began. They were gone within a few months; right?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: The fact is that some left. A majority of those people remained and they continued working. They didn't leave because somebody had ordered them to do so. Some believed that the area was not safe and they sought out solutions in some other parts of our former state.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sir, at paragraph 11 of your statement you state that during the war most members of the special police unit were conscientious and responsible men who did not commit offences, and you state that members of the unit were removed for disciplinary reasons including committing crimes. Now, the truth is that the Banja Luka CSB special police unit was well known for its criminality and its members were not properly punished for their crimes; right?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Well, I would not agree with you. In that period those who had a lack of discipline or did not respect the command, they were sent away from the unit and it was up to the judiciary to initiate further proceedings. About 40 persons were sent out of the unit because of certain actions that were not in accordance with the code of conduct of the police or the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could have D4139, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, this is a report from Simo Drljaca from the Prijedor SJB to the Banja Luka CSB, and you have seen this before. And as you can see, it describes rampant misconduct by special police unit members under a member by the name of Strazivuk who were arbitrarily arresting, interrogating, and abusing prisoners at the Omarska camp, and towards the end of the report it also refers to the -- to complaints about the conduct of the special unit and their looting during moping-up operations. Now, this reference to Mr. Strazivuk, that's Slobodan Strazivuk who was a member of the special police unit; right?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: I assume that that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now in your statement you blame crimes in Prijedor detention facilitates on paramilitaries, but in fact as this report shows, members of the Banja Luka CSB special police units stood out even by Omarska standards for the criminal behaviour there; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about this. I know that part of the members there did certain illegal things, but the main problem in respect of these illegal things was that in that area, along with some unconscientious members, there were some members of units -- different units that had withdrawn from Slovenia and Croatia and that did some of these illegal things and were not under the control either of the army or the police and that was the main problem. That is why there were certain activities and plans to bring an end to such things. Therefore, a decision was made that all paramilitary units, special units, and some that were self-styled, that they should all be disbanded and that at the level of Republika Srpska a single unit would be formed that would be under a single command, and that practically it would include only persons - that was the decision --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: -- that was there anyway --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I interrupted you because you were moving away from my question which was about this particular incident which I would like to get back to. My next question relates to this as well. Mr. Strazivuk continued to operate as a special unit member even after this information was sent to the CSB chief about his failure to control the criminal behaviour of his subordinates; right?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Well, in that period there were certain conflicts between Mr. Simo Drljaca and the members of the special detachment, and there were some rumours, I guess that was by way of justification, that the forces that Drljaca had at his disposal were also involved in some of these activities that were not in line, so there were some clashes in that regard. And then everything, I mean, was ascribed to the special unit, everything that was not regular. This was some kind of internal investigation that was underway, I think. Otherwise, the communication between the CSB and the centre in Prijedor was not normal. Often, there were certain problems and there were certain illegal things that were done by Mr. Drljaca, because, as a matter of fact, he even seized -- seized equipment from our people without having the authority to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sir, your answer is not even remotely connected to my question, responsive to my question, which was: Slobodan Strazivuk continued to operate as a special unit member even after this information was sent to the CSB chief about his failure to control the criminal behaviour of his subordinates; right?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Well, specifically this information was sent to the chief of the centre. It didn't go down to me. I cannot say how this investigation was completed, and the chief of the centre probably rounded all of this off. Now, whether this is correct or not correct, but if this man is on the list of members of that unit, that means that he stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 3 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we show the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Under number 44, we see Slobodan Strazivuk receiving and signing for his salary in August 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Yes. But that is a right that had been agreed upon for all members of the unit, regardless of whether they were in the unit at that moment. Because when it was disbanded in mid-July, after that it was stated that they would all get this one salary for August, regardless of whether they were there or not because allegedly that is what was decided. I don't know who it was that made the decision, but the decision was made that they should be paid from the resources of the centre up until August. And that is when the centre no longer had any obligation towards them. Now at that moment, whether Strazivuk was still in the unit or not, that I don't know. I only know -- well, from this list one can see that active personnel were not receiving salaries that we were actually linked to the centre and not to the unit, financially speaking, because we exercised all our status-related rights at the centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now in your previous answer you referred to an investigation into this misconduct in Omarska by special unit members. The truth is there were no disciplinary proceedings initiated in relation to this incident; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: I do not know what was done, what was done by superior people. At any rate if this information arrived, somebody had to take that into account and somebody must have done that work in terms of ascertaining the truth concerning that dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go back to 65 ter 25977, please, page 364.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And again, sir, this is your prior testimony. And at line 21, you're being asked about the report we just saw from Drljaca to Zupljanin about the misconduct of the special unit. And you're asked: "This is somewhat ironically, I suppose, one could say a complaint from Simo Drljaca on the 13th of June where we hear the same theme. The unit whose members were commanded by the gentleman who is named there was not able to control any -- exert any control over the conduct of his troops. That was the main reason why the troops assigned duties as Omarska," if we go to the next page, "behaved with such extreme negligence. What they did there had least of all to do with security." And she's reading -- the lawyer is reading from the document. And at line 8, she says: "Now, this was addressed to Stojan Zupljanin. Did he pass that complaint on to you to investigate?" And you answer: "This was not conveyed to me personally. "I'm trying to remember. I think that there was some kind of back and forth between the special and local police. They were quarrelling, so it turned out to be a quarrel between them. I think that both of them behaved improperly, but there were stories. I think somebody did conduct that procedure. I think this was on the 13th of June. "I don't remember any disciplinary proceedings on this matter. I don't remember conducting anything like that. It was probably at the time when there was nobody there to do that." Now your prior testimony stating that you weren't aware of any disciplinary proceedings into this incident is correct; right?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: I said now as well that I assumed that higher instances were resolving that and I also said that there was this conflict between the police of Prijedor and of Banja Luka, between Simo Drljaca and Stojan Zupljanin, that there was not good communication in terms of co-operation, and that there were problems. I specifically know that our two operatives were almost arrested --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: -- when they asked to have it established who was driving a car that had not been registered and that had been stolen in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I was simply asking you to confirm your prior testimony on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender these two pages as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add them to Exhibit P6653.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to D1562, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And again, sir, you've seen this document before which is a report from the Banja Luka -- sorry, from the Banja Luka SJB to the Banja Luka CSB alleging that four members of the Banja Luka CSB special police detachment committed the crime of robbery and aggravated theft; in particular, by stealing a car of -- belonged to a person by the name of Amir Durgutovic. Now that person was a Muslim; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And it states that criminal reports were filed against four special unit members: Radomir Boskan -- who is on page 2 of both languages: Radomir Boskan, Miroslav Dragojevic [phoen], Ljubomir Jokic, and Dusan Dragojevic [phoen]. Now these four special detachment members were arrested and they were shortly thereafter broken out of gaol by other special detachment members; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to D1801, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a report on that prison breakout in the publication "Glas," and the report goes down -- largely down the left-hand -- far left column, and this is from July 23rd, so two days after the criminal reports were filed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the second page in the English and the top of the third column in the B/C/S. If we could just scroll up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in the third column from the left --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Next one over, actually. There is a quote from Mr. Ecim which goes on to the next column as well, so if we could zoom out a little bit to see what's on the --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And Ecim is talking about the breakout. He says the job was done in five minutes and we released Jokic and Dragojevic without a bullet being fired. Now it's clear, is it not, that, as this article indicates, the breakout of the special police members from prison was at the very least approved by the deputy commander of the unit, Ljuban Ecim; right?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: That is not correct. Now I'm going to tell you what the problem is there. I have already spoken about that. There was a conflict between Tutus, Vladimir, and Stojan Zupljanin. And there was this power struggle between the two them in Banja Luka. Within this struggle there was this media game in terms of providing different information. It is a fact that the vehicle in question was illegal. So this -- at least that's what I was told. This gentleman did not have proper documents for that vehicle, but that was a pretext for rising tensions. And also it was a power game, to show who was more powerful in town, the chief of the centre of the public security services or of the security services in general. So the fact is that there was this release and, as far as I know, without the consent of the command this was done by some members of that unit together with some other supporters of theirs from the military. So practically, without any gun-fire they entered the prison and they got these people out in contravention of prescribed standards. But the essence of all of this was the conflict in general. There was this conflict of sorts between these local chiefs of the public security station and the chief of the centre because everybody wanted to be the man in charge in his own territory and his own town and that nobody could influence his decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, the quote I just read you from Mr. Ecim was: "The job was done in five minutes and we released Jokic and Dragojevic without a bullet being fired." Don't you agree that that reflects his approval of this breakout?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Well, obviously you haven't read the entire text. It says here, very nicely, that people of their own initiative decided on this release, and they did that within a few minutes without a single bullet being fired; that is to say, there were no victims. And it says here, very nicely, that none of the members of the command had approved of this activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you point me to where it says "none of the members of this command had approved this activity"?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: Well, if you understand our language: People on their own initiative without anyone's approval decided to break out. This job, or as we call it, was done in five minutes, and they were freed without a single bullet being fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you agree this article does not state: "None of the members of this command had approved this activity"?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: That's what I said. That's what I just said. It's written here in the article, and it also says here that we went to see Stojan Zupljanin around 2.30 in the morning and warned him that people had decided to attack. All right, there were some indications that might happen and thanks to Zupljanin we didn't do that. He gave us a firm promise --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: -- that the people would be released.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: And then it follows as I described. People on their own initiative --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Again, you're moving away from my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, my time is nearly up. I can conclude in 10 to 15 minutes. I have two brief topics to cover, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your statement you claim that Stojan Zupljanin's orders to the SJBs, including orders to Prijedor, Kljuc, and Sanski Most were not respected and exactly the opposite of what he ordered was done. Now, given your position at the time, I take it you were not directly involved in the issuing of Zupljanin's orders to the SJBs or ensuring that they were implemented; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: I was not involved, but I received information about the situation in the field because I had friendly sources in these centres and I knew what the general sentiment was and how they behaved when they received certain requests from the centre. There was a tendency not to obey orders from the centre and local mandarins imposed themselves as the only interpreters of whatever came from above and the only ones who decided about certain activities. They were little sultans in their own little fiefdoms.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber has received evidence of Mr. Drljaca, for example, in Prijedor responding immediately to Mr. Zupljanin's dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Examples would be P5471, P5518, P3968, and D1865.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In light of your previous answer, I won't go into these dispatches, but I will ask you if you are able to identify any concrete example of a specific order by Mr. Zupljanin that was not respected by one of the SJBs that you identify?

utterances.speaker: KW426
utterances.text: If I tell you that Mr. Drljaca practically arrested our men in Prijedor when they came to insist that measures be applied to one person who seized an AT vehicle from Banja Luka and drove it around Prijedor without any license number, their communication devices were seized from them and they practically ran away from Prijedor to avoid further embarrassment and problems. If you took these documents from the security services centre, you will see that an Official Note was made about this incident. Two of our men and owners of the car were mistreated in Prijedor by Simo Drljaca and the inspector who is in charge of car theft. If that is not an example of the disrespect shown to the security services centre and its employees who, in the hierarchy should be higher, I really don't know what proof you would recognise. There was genuine disrespect by these lower-ranked stations and centres vis-a-vis the centre in Banja Luka. That was a general rule. I said that before and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, again, you didn't respond to my question, so let me ask it this way: You're -- this claim of yours about the dysfunction in the hierarchy is based on nothing more than rumours; right? You don't have any concrete evidence to support that Mr. Zupljanin's orders were not followed by the SJBs?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It couldn't be more specific than the example the witness just gave. It couldn't possibly be more specific. Members of the security services centre were mistreated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in the public security station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, your objection is overruled. Please continue. Or can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that adequate action was not taken regarding the illegal activities committed by members of the Prijedor centre in the Koricani area. An investigation was ordered. It was ordered that all the bodies be recovered and returned to Prijedor, but as far as I know Mr. Drljaca did not comply. If that is not enough, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 25976, page 16 in both languages. And this should not be shown to the public, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And just to orient you, sir, this is from your -- the interview you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2002, and I'd like to direct your attention to the first question at the top of the page. In your language, this is about halfway down in the English. And about halfway through that question you're asked: "Now do you agree or disagree with that statement by Mr. Zupljanin, that that was in fact a true statement that his orders were effectively the law once they had been issued orally or written." And you answer: "I think not." And then you're asked to explain why it would be permissible to ignore an order made by Stojan Zupljanin. And you say: "These were strange times.
